physical_harm: Death caused by burns and shock
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the appellant-accused poured kerosene on the deceased when she was trying to run out of the house to save herself and set her ablaze by throwing a match-stick on her person.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, including the dying declaration of the deceased, as credible and stated that the accused was conscious and aware of his actions during the incident.

legal_representation.accused: Sushil Karanjkar, Nikhilesh Kumar and K. N. Rai, Advs.
legal_representation.state: Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar and Anoop Kandari, Advs.

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused's act of pouring kerosene on the deceased and setting her ablaze was a deliberate and premeditated act, constituting culpable homicide amounting to murder under Section 300 fourthly of the IPC. They emphasized that the accused was fully conscious and aware of the dangerous nature of his actions, and that the subsequent act of pouring water was an attempt to conceal guilt rather than a mitigating factor.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the death of the deceased was culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and the case should fall under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC. They contended that the accused was under the influence of liquor, lacked the intention to kill, and attempted to save the deceased by pouring water, which should mitigate the offence to Section 304 Part II IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the intention to kill is a crucial factor in determining whether an act constitutes murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The court emphasized that the accused's awareness of the dangerous consequences of his actions is key to determining the nature of the offence.
precedent_relied_upon: Kalu Ram v. State of Rajasthan (2000) 10 SCC 324; Santosh v. State of Maharashtra (2015) 7 SCC 641; Bhagwan Tukaram Dange v. State of Maharashtra (2014) 4 SCC 270
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the court found that the accused's actions constituted murder under Section 300 fourthly of the IPC, and the aggravating factors outweighed any mitigating factors.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The court considered the deliberate and premeditated nature of the act, the awareness of the dangerous consequences, and the lack of any evidence of the accused being in a highly inebriated state.
